If you want to save the cross just to reuse it again in R, it's best to use save() and load():

  save(diaTEST, file="diaTEST.RData")

  load("diaTEST.RData")

If you write the cross to a CSV file, there's no way, currently, to have the genotypes written as A/H/B. But in your call to read.cross, you can use genotypes=c("AA", "AB", "BB"). You can leave off estimate.map=TRUE; that's only used if there is no map in the csv file, and there should be, following orderMarkers.

  diaTESTmap <- read.cross("csv", ".", "diaTESTmap.csv", genotypes=c("AA", "AB", "BB"))

karl

messages.subject: stepwiseqtl and refining mqms
messages.body_plain:
Hi all, and Karl,

I'm fitting multiple qtl models to an eQTL dataset, looking for additional loci and epistasis (beyond single local/distant effects).
For the most part, results from stepwiseqtl look pretty sensible and interesting, but I'm getting plenty of screwy results too and am thinking about how best to refine the output. There's ~1/3 or so (of 370 predicted interactions) where the number of individuals is severely imbalanced (often from a case of segregation distortion that effects half of chromosome 1 - I'll drop these markers in future - but many others where very tightly linked qtl are predicted). A couple examples are attached.

What's the best way to deal with these? Usually the main additive effect dominates the interaction so the pLOD is no help, and I don't see any measure of confidence based on the number of individuals. Shouldn't these be penalised in some way during model selection?
If I operate on the qtl object from stepwiseqtl to drop a position (e.g. where confidence intervals overlap) this kills the interaction terms in the formula, so for now I'm just parsing the results and rebuilding from scratch, hard filtering on individual counts. Is there a better way?
As for significance, is it appropriate to use an empirical pLOD threshold generated from permuted data? I'm using initial penalties from scantwo permutations for selection, but I still need to control fdr right?

Finally, should I be looking at other methods in rqtl (mqm - I've had errors due to map expansion after augmentation so haven't pursued this) or elsewhere for assessing hotspots? I've been playing with qtlhot and random forests.

Thanks for your advice,
Luke

messages.body_plain:
To assess the precision of QTL localization, look at the region in which the LOD score is within some value of its maximum, rather than the region that is above the significance threshold.

Let LOD(p) be the LOD score at position p, and let M = max LOD(p), the maximum LOD score.
For a 1.5-LOD support interval, you'd take the positions p for which LOD(p) > M - 1.5.

You can use the function lodint(), which is similar to the function bayesint().

karl

Is this possible at all? If yes, how does one get for example two confidence intervals for two QTLs on the same chromosome, as currently if running for example bayesint() the output is always one confidence interval, even if I have two significant peaks?

You can lodint and bayesint on a QTL object, if you've applied refineqtl so that it contains profile LOD scores.
But it's probably better, for a pair of linked QTL, to use a 2-QTL scan and provide a confidence region.
R/qtl doesn't contain code to help with this, though.

If you have access to the R/qtl book (http://www.rqtl.org/book), see Figure 11.15 on page 352.

> 2. Pleiotropy
>
> You once mentioned looking at overlaps of confidence intervals as evidence for/against a common QTL, isn’t the best approach and then suggested a combined analysis.
>
> What do you mean by combined analysis?

Analyse the phenotypes jointly, for example by the method of Knott and Haley (2000; http://www.genetics.org/content/156/2/899.short) or Jiang and Zeng (1995; http://www.genetics.org/content/140/3/1111.short)

> 3. In your publication (A simple regression-based method to map quantitative trait loci underlying function-valued phenotypes) on the usage of SLOD/MLOD, I would have the following questions:
> 	• Can this analysis also include same phenotypes over different treatments?

potentially

> 	• Can one account for pleiotropy using this approach?

it is trying to account for pleiotropy, in that we expect a given locus to affect the phenotype at multiple time points.

> 	• How are confidence intervals for a unique QTL calculated once identified with either SLOD or MLOD?

I don't yet have a solution to this problem.

> 	• Can this approach be used amongst two mapping populations?

I suppose.

karl
